subjective.question: Define the following: (i) const keyword (ii) Reference variable (iii) Dangling reference
subjective.answer: Const keyword: The const keyword is used for something to be constant. The actual meaning depends on where it occurs, but it generally means something is to be held constant. There can be constant functions, constant variables or parameters, etc. Reference variable: The references are pointers internally; actually they are constant pointers. You cannot perform any kind of arithmetic manipulation with references that you normally do with pointers. Dangling reference: The pointer to an object (when the object has already been deallocated or released) is called a dangling pointer/reference.

subjective.question: How can the dangling reference problem be avoided?
subjective.answer: To avoid a dangling reference, don't return the reference of a local variable (transient) from a function.

subjective.question: Why do we use reference variables? Give one example. (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: C++ references allow you to create a second name for a variable that you can use to read or modify the original data stored in that variable. Example: int x; int& foo = x; // foo is now a reference to x, so this sets x to 56 foo = 56; std::cout << x << std::endl;

subjective.question: For the public part of the Throttle class declaration below, mark each function member header as follows: mark C for any constructor; mark X for any function that is forbidden from changing the throttle's data fields. class Throttle { public: Throttle( ); Throttle(int size); void shut_off( ); void shift(int amount); double flow( ) const; bool is_on( ) const; ... } (Marks: 6)
subjective.answer: Throttle( ); — C (constructor) Throttle(int size); — C (constructor) void shut_off( ); — neither (it can change the data fields) void shift(int amount); — neither (it can change the data fields) double flow( ) const; — X (const function: forbidden from changing the data fields) bool is_on( ) const; — X (const function: forbidden from changing the data fields) The two Throttle(...) members are constructors because they have the same name as the class and no return type. The functions declared with const at the end (flow and is_on) are not allowed to modify the object's data members, so they are marked X.

subjective.question: Give short answers to the following: 1. Why does a List waste less memory as compared to Arrays? 2. Why can we change the size of a list after its creation when we cannot do that in simple arrays? (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: 1. Linked lists do not need contiguous blocks of memory; extremely large data sets stored in an array might not be able to fit in memory. Linked list storage does not need to be preallocated (again, due to arrays needing contiguous memory blocks). Inserting or removing an element into a linked list requires one data update, whereas inserting or removing an element into an array requires n updates (all elements after the modified index need to be shifted). An array is a collection of the same data type; in a linked list there are two fields, one is the data (address/value) field and the other is the pointer field, and in an array the elements are arranged in a specific order. 2. The answer is similar to part 1: inserting or removing an element into a linked list requires one data update, while in an array it requires shifting all elements after the modified index. The size of an array is mentioned with its declaration and its elements are in contiguous positions, one after another. In a linked list, we give the address of the next element in the next part of the node, so nodes can be added or removed at any time and the size can change after creation.

subjective.question: What is Function Call Stack? Give a short answer. (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Stacks play a key role in the implementation of function calls in programming languages. In C++, for example, the "call stack" is used to pass function arguments and receive return values. The call stack is also used for local variables.

subjective.question: Give one benefit of using a Stack. (Marks: 1)
subjective.answer: In computer science, a stack is a Last In First Out (LIFO) abstract data type and data structure. A stack can have any abstract data type as an element, but is characterized by only two fundamental operations: push and pop. The data structure itself enforces the proper order of calls.

subjective.question: What is meant by an empty stack? (Marks: 1)
subjective.answer: Empty stack means that there is no element on the stack. The isEmpty() boolean function returns true if the stack is empty, false otherwise.

subjective.question: I am going to execute this code with THREE pushes and ONE pop: Stack s; s.push(1); s.push(2); s.push(3); cout << s.pop( ); Suppose that the stack s is represented by a singly linked list. Draw the linked list after the above operations and show where the top element is in the list. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: The pop removes the most recently pushed element, so cout prints 3. In the linked-list representation the elements are inserted at the head, so after the pop the list is: head --> [ 2 ] --> [ 1 ] --> NULL The top element of the stack is at the head of the list, i.e. the node containing 2.

subjective.question: Why is a queue called a linear data structure?
subjective.answer: A queue is a linear data structure into which items can only be inserted at one end and removed from the other. In contrast to the stack, which is a LIFO (Last In First Out) structure, a queue is a FIFO (First In First Out) structure.

subjective.question: What is the function of the length() method in the Queue?
subjective.answer: In Queue, the length() method has a single statement, i.e. "return size;". This method returns the size of the queue, reflecting the number of elements in the queue. It is not the size of the array used internally to store the elements of the queue.

subjective.question: Give the names of the basic Queue operations. (Marks: 1)
subjective.answer: The queue data structure supports the following operations: • enqueue(X) — Place X at the rear of the queue. • dequeue() — Remove the front element and return it. • front() — Return the front element without removing it. • isEmpty() — Return TRUE if the queue is empty, FALSE otherwise.

subjective.question: Which process places data at the back of the queue? (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: enqueue(X) — it places X at the rear/back of the queue.

subjective.question: Describe any two uses of priority queues. (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Priority queues are used at many places, especially in operating systems. In operating systems, we have a queue of different processes. If some process comes with higher priority, it will be processed first; here we have seen a variation of queue. We also use the priority queue in simulation: the events will be inserted in the queue and the event going to occur first in future will be popped.

subjective.question: Describe the use of Queues.
subjective.answer: Out of the numerous uses of queues, one of the most useful is simulation. A simulation program attempts to model a real-world phenomenon. Many popular video games are simulations, e.g. SimCity, Flight Simulator, etc. Each object and action in the simulation has a counterpart in the real world. Computer simulation is a very powerful tool and is used in different high-tech industries, especially in engineering projects; for example, it is used in aeroplane manufacturing. Computer simulation is actually a full-fledged subject of Computer Science and contains very complex mathematics sometimes, e.g. simulation of computer networks, traffic networks, etc.

subjective.question: Complete the body of this function. Use a Queue of characters to store the input line as it is being read. int counter( ) // Precondition: There is a line of input waiting to be read from cin. // Postcondition: A line of input has been read from cin, up to but not including the newline character. The return value of the function is the number of times that the LAST character of the line appeared somewhere in this line. // EXAMPLE: Input: PQQYDYYTY — the value returned would be 4, since there are 4 Y's in the input line. (Marks: 10)
subjective.answer: The function reads the line, enqueues every character, then dequeues the characters one by one and counts how many of them are equal to the last character of the line: int counter() { char a[100]; int i = 0; int answer = 0; Queue q; cin.getline(a, 98, '\n'); for (i = 0; i < strlen(a); i++) { q.enqueue(a[i]); } i--; while (!q.isEmpty()) { if (a[i] == q.dequeue()) { answer++; } } return answer; }

subjective.question: I am going to execute this code with THREE inserts (enqueue) and ONE remove (dequeue): Queue s; s.insert(1); s.insert(2); s.insert(3); cout << s.remove( ); Suppose that queue s is represented by a circular array. Draw the state of the private member variables "data" and "front" of s after the above code. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: The remove() takes out the element at the front, so cout prints 1. The three inserted values were stored in the circular array starting at index 0; after removing the front element (1), the state is: data: index 0 = (removed) index 1 = 2 index 2 = 3 (remaining positions empty) front = 1 So the queue now holds 2 and 3, with the front pointing at index 1 (the element 2).

subjective.question: How do we evaluate postfix expressions? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Evaluating a postfix expression: • Each operator in a postfix expression refers to the previous two operands. • Each time we read an operand, we push it on a stack. • When we reach an operator, we pop the two operands from the top of the stack, apply the operator and push the result back on the stack.

subjective.question: Trace the running of the infix to postfix conversion algorithm on the infix expression A * (B - C) / D. (Marks: 10)
subjective.answer: Scanning the expression from left to right, each operand is written directly to the postfix output, while operators are pushed onto the stack according to precedence and are popped when a closing parenthesis is found or the expression ends. Step-by-step trace (Symbol | Postfix | Stack): A | A | — ; * | A | * ; ( | A | *( ; B | AB | *( ; - | AB | *(- ; C | ABC | *(- ; ) | ABC- | * ; / | ABC-* | / ; D | ABC-*D | / ; End | ABC-*D/ | — Final postfix expression: ABC-*D/

subjective.question: Consider the CList and Node classes defined as follows: class Node { public: Node *next; Node *prev; int data; }; class CList { public: void insertHead(int); void insertTail(int); void removeHead(); void removeTail(); bool isEmpty(); bool find(int); private: Node *head; Node *tail; }; A. Write the body of the member function insertHead, which inserts a new element at the head of the list. B. Write the body of the member function removeTail, which removes the element at the tail of the list. (Marks: 10)
subjective.answer: A. insertHead creates a new node; if the list is empty it becomes both head and tail, otherwise it is linked before the current head: B. removeTail removes the tail node; if there is only one node both head and tail become NULL, otherwise the tail moves one node back: void CList::insertHead(int x) { Node *newNode = new Node(); newNode->data = x; newNode->next = NULL; newNode->prev = NULL; if (isEmpty()) head = tail = newNode; else { newNode->next = head; newNode->prev = NULL; head->prev = newNode; head = newNode; } } void CList::removeTail(int &x) { if (isEmpty()) return; else { Node *p = tail; if (head == tail) head = tail = NULL; else { tail = tail->prev; tail->next = NULL; } x = p->data; delete p; return; } }

subjective.question: What is a binary tree? Brief it.
subjective.answer: "A binary tree is a finite set of elements that is either empty or is partitioned into three disjoint subsets. The first subset contains a single element called the root of the tree. The other two subsets are themselves binary trees, called the left and right sub-trees."

subjective.question: What is a complete binary tree?
subjective.answer: A complete binary tree of depth d is the strictly binary tree all of whose leaves are at level d. (Another paper in the same file phrases it as: a binary tree in which every node must have exactly two children if it is an internal node, and zero children if it is a leaf node.)

subjective.question: Describe the following: (i) Height of tree (ii) Balance of Node
subjective.answer: (i) Height of tree: The height of a binary tree is the maximum level of its leaves (also called the depth). (ii) Balance of Node: The balance of a node in a binary search tree is defined as the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. In other words, at a particular node, the difference in heights of its left and right subtrees gives the balance of the node.

subjective.question: How can we perform level-order traversal on a tree?
subjective.answer: We can print a binary tree level by level by employing a recursive or non-recursive method. The idea of a level-order traversal is to visit the root, then visit all nodes "1 level away" from the root (left to right), then all nodes "2 levels away" from the root, etc. A level-order traversal requires using a queue (rather than a recursive algorithm, which implicitly uses a stack). A queue is a FIFO structure, which can make the level-order traversal easier.

subjective.question: What are the applications of Binary Tree? (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: The binary tree is a useful data structure for rapidly storing sorted data and rapidly retrieving stored data. It can hold objects that are sorted by their keys. It can represent a structured object: an operating system maintains a disk's file system as a tree, where file folders act as tree nodes.

subjective.question: Here is a small binary tree: the root is A; A's left child is B and right child is E; B has only a right child D; D has only a left child C; E has only a left child G; G's left child is F and right child is I; F has only a right child H. Write the order of the nodes visited in: a) A post-order traversal (L, R, N) b) A level-order traversal (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: a) Post-order traversal: C D B H F I G E A b) Level-order traversal: A B E D G C F I H

subjective.question: Here is a small binary tree: the root is 14; 14's left child is 2 and right child is 11; 2's left child is 1 and right child is 3; 11's left child is 10 and right child is 30; 10 has only a left child 7; 30 has only a right child 40. A. What are all the leaves? (2 pts) B. What are the ancestors of the node 30? (2 pts) C. What are the descendants of the node 11? (2 pts) D. Is the tree a binary search tree (BST)? (true/false) (2 pts) E. Print the tree when visited in in-order manner. (5 pts) (Marks: 13)
subjective.answer: A. Leaves of the tree = 1, 3, 7, 40 B. Ancestors of the node 30 = 11, 14 C. Descendants of the node 11 = 10, 30, 7, 40 D. Is the tree a binary search tree (BST)? False E. In-order traversal = 1, 2, 3, 14, 7, 10, 11, 30, 40

subjective.question: How can we delete a node with two children in a binary search tree using its right subtree?
subjective.answer: The node to be deleted has a left child (subtree) and a right child (subtree). In this case we bypass the node in such a way that we find the inorder successor of this node (from its right subtree) and then link the parent of the node to be deleted to this successor node. Thus the node is deleted.

subjective.question: What is the maximum number of comparisons we have to perform during insertion in a BST?
subjective.answer: If we have a complete binary tree with n numbers of nodes, the depth d of the tree can be found by the following equation: d = log2(n + 1) - 1 If the tree is complete binary or near-to-complete, we need log2(n) number of comparisons. Whereas in a linked list, the comparisons required could be a maximum of n.

subjective.question: How is a single left rotation performed in an AVL tree?
subjective.answer: This rotation is almost similar to the single right rotation. We start from tree node k1: k1 is the root while tree node k2 is its right child. Due to the left rotation, the right child k2 of the root k1 will become the root, and k1 will go down to become the left child of k2.

subjective.question: Explain the two cases in which we apply double rotation in an AVL tree.
subjective.answer: Sometimes a single rotation is not sufficient to balance an unbalanced tree. The two cases are the following: 1. Insertion into the right subtree of the left child of X node (RL case) 2. Insertion into the left subtree of the right child of X node (LR case)

subjective.question: What is the difference between a binary tree and an AVL tree?
subjective.answer: An AVL tree is identical to a BST, barring the following possible differences: • Height of the left and right subtrees may differ by at most 1. • Height of an empty tree is defined to be (-1).

subjective.question: What is the similarity between an AVL tree and a Binary Search Tree, and how is an AVL tree different from a Binary Search Tree?
subjective.answer: Similarity: An AVL tree is a self-balancing binary search tree, so it has the same node ordering as a BST: each node has at most two children (left and right), and the keys in the left subtree are smaller and in the right subtree are greater than the node's key. A binary tree is a tree data structure in which each node has at most two children, typically called left and right; one common use of binary trees is binary search trees, another is binary heaps. Difference: In an AVL tree, the heights of the two child sub-trees of any node differ by at most one; therefore it is also called height-balanced. Lookup, insertion and deletion all take O(log n) time in both the average and worst cases. Additions and deletions may require the tree to be rebalanced by one or more tree rotations.

subjective.question: Is the following statement correct? If your answer is No, then correct it. "A tree is an AVL tree if at least half of the nodes fulfill the AVL condition." (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: The statement is wrong. The correct statement is: A tree is an AVL tree if ALL the nodes fulfill the AVL condition.
